unit.title: Cut fit and install trunking system

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to plan, cut, fit, install and check trunking systems in PVC and steel. You will choose the right system for the conditions, work out capacity and quantities, keep different systems segregated and fire walls sealed, and make sound bends, joints and board entries. You will also keep the earth path of steel trunking continuous, test it, and lead a team through inspection and handover.

blocks.p: Trunking is an enclosure with a removable lid. Cables are **laid in**, not pulled through, so circuits can be added, changed and inspected for the whole life of the building. This unit is for Level 3 trainees and electricians who plan and lead trunking work: you read the drawings, choose the system, do the calculations, guide the team, and inspect, test and record the finished job.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Read drawings and specifications
Find the trunking type, size, finish, route, height, fill limit, segregation, fire-stopping and earthing requirements. Raise a written query when two drawings disagree.
Survey and plan the route
Walk the route. Find obstacles, other services, fire-rated walls, expansion joints and wall materials. Agree the route and the order of work with the other trades.
Choose the trunking and fittings
Pick PVC, steel or stainless steel, and dado, mini, lighting, underfloor or bench trunking, to suit the heat, sun, salt air and use of the place.
Work out capacity and quantities
Use a fill limit or cable factors, leave spare space, and remember grouping. Prepare a take-off with a waste allowance and cost it.
Plan safe work and lead the team
Isolate circuits in or near the work, scan before drilling, control dust and work at height, brief the team and set hold points.
Measure, cut and form
Mark every length from one measured plan, cut square, remove burrs, make site-made bends, and use factory fittings where they are the better choice.
Fix, join and enter boards
Fix level and plumb at the maker's spacing, join with couplers, allow for expansion, and enter boards and boxes with proper fittings.
Keep systems segregated and fire-safe
Keep dividers continuous, give fire alarm and data their own compartments, and seal trunking inside and outside at fire-rated walls and floors.
Earth and test steel trunking
Fit earth links, connect the run to the earth bar, test continuity with a low-resistance ohmmeter and record the readings.
Inspect, hand over and record
Inspect against the drawing, list and correct defects, mark up the as-built drawing and hand over the records.

blocks.p: The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US National Electrical Code (NEC), but on site and in suppliers' catalogues you will hear British trade words too. Know both.

head: British trade term
NEC (US) term
Meaning
rows: Steel trunking
Metal wireway (an auxiliary gutter, when it serves a board)
A sheet-metal enclosure with a removable or hinged cover, into which cables are laid.
PVC trunking
Nonmetallic wireway
The same idea in PVC.
Mini-trunking, dado trunking
Surface raceway; a multioutlet assembly when it carries outlets
Small or decorative surface trunking, usually with a clip-on lid.
Underfloor trunking
Underfloor raceway
Flat ducts in or under the floor, with outlet boxes at set points.
Space factor, cable factor
Conductor fill
How much of the trunking's inside space the cables may take up.
Circuit protective conductor (CPC), earth
Equipment grounding conductor (EGC), ground
The conductor that connects metal parts back to the earth bar at the board.

blocks.note: A new or altered installation must be inspected and certified before JPS will connect it. This is overseen by the Government Electrical Regulator (GER), and the inspection is done by a licensed electrical inspector. The trunking is part of that installation, so its fill, segregation, fire stopping and earthing can all be checked. JPS supplies 110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The sections follow a real job, from choosing the system to handing it over. Work through the examples with a calculator, then try the practice test and read every explanation. Figures that vary by maker or by job are given as typical values: the specification, the maker's data and your instructor always come first.

head: Type
What it is
Best used for
Watch out for
rows: PVC mini-trunking
Small PVC channel with a clip-on lid, sometimes with a self-adhesive back
Adding one or two circuits in a finished room without cutting chases
Adhesive backs let go on dusty, damp or hot walls, so screw it as well. Very little space inside.
Dado and skirting trunking
Wide, neat trunking at desk or skirting height, usually with two or three compartments; outlets clip into it
Offices, laboratories and classrooms that need power and data outlets along the walls
The divider must be continuous, and outlet boxes need dividers too.
Steel trunking
Sheet steel, galvanised or painted, from about 50 × 50 mm upwards, with a screwed or clip-on lid
Factories, plant rooms, risers and anywhere strength is needed
Sharp cut edges, weight, and the earth path across every joint.
Lighting trunking
Steel channel hung below a roof, which carries the cables and supports the light fittings
Warehouses, workshops and supermarkets
It must hang from the structure on supports rated for the fittings as well as the cables.
Underfloor trunking
Flat steel ducts in the floor screed or under a raised floor, with outlet boxes at set points
Open-plan offices and banking halls, so desks can be supplied at many points
Outlet positions are fixed early; lids must keep out water from floor cleaning.
Bench trunking
Trunking fixed along a bench, with segregated sections and outlets
Laboratory, workshop and classroom benches
Knocks, spills and chemicals.
Stainless steel trunking
Steel that resists rust without a coating
Kitchens, food plants and sea-front sites
Cost, and the need for stainless fixings.

head: Fitting
What it does
rows: Flat bend
Turns the run across the face of the wall or ceiling. The lid stays in one flat plane.
Internal angle
Takes the run into the inside corner between two walls.
External angle
Takes the run round an outside corner.
Tee and cross
A tee takes a branch off the run; a cross joins four runs.
Reducer
Joins two sizes of trunking.
Coupler
Joins two lengths. On steel trunking it usually carries the earth link.
End cap
Closes the end of a run so cables are protected and nothing gets in.
Flanged adaptor
Joins the trunking to a distribution board or box, covers the cut edges and keeps the earth path.
Outlet box
Holds socket or data outlets on dado trunking. In multi-compartment trunking it has a divider.
Cable retainers
Straps, bridges or pin racks that hold the cables in when the lid is off, or when the lid faces down or the run is vertical.
Fire barrier
Seals the inside of the trunking where it passes through a fire-rated wall or floor.
Expansion coupler
Lets two lengths slide a little as they heat and cool.

blocks.h: Choosing the material for the conditions

blocks.p: At Level 3 you are expected to choose, and to explain your choice. Ask four questions: What are the conditions? What must the trunking carry, now and later? How should it look and how will the room be used? What do the specification and the maker's data say?

head: Condition
What it does
A good choice
rows: Heat: cooking ranges, boilers, hot roof spaces
PVC softens, sags and warps. Many makers give ordinary PVC trunking an upper limit of about 60 °C. Heat also lowers the current the cables may carry.
Steel or stainless steel, routed away from the hottest places. The designer applies rating factors to the cables.
Strong sunlight
Ultraviolet (UV) light makes ordinary PVC chalky and brittle, so it cracks.
PVC made and marked for outdoor use (UV-stabilised), or metal. Keep the run in shade where you can.
Salt air near the sea
Plain steel rusts quickly. Rust at joints can break the earth path.
Hot-dip galvanised steel with cut edges treated, stainless steel, or outdoor PVC, with matching fixings.
Steam, grease and washing down
Dirt and water get into joints; grease is a fire risk.
Steel or stainless steel with well-fitting lids, kept clear of cooking equipment.
Knocks from trolleys, forklifts and stock
PVC cracks and lids come off.
Steel, mounted out of reach or protected.
Escape routes and public areas
Burning PVC gives off thick smoke and toxic, corrosive fumes.
Metal trunking, or low-smoke materials, where the specification asks for them.
Offices and classrooms
Mild conditions; looks and flexibility matter.
PVC dado trunking with separate compartments. It needs no earthing.

blocks.note: Much of Jamaica's building work is close to the sea, and the sun is strong all year. A wall that faces the afternoon sun, or a roof space under metal sheeting, can be far hotter than the air outside. Indoor PVC that would last for decades in an air-conditioned office in New Kingston can be brittle within a few years on a sea-front wall in Negril or Port Antonio.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: When two different metals touch in damp or salty air, one of them corrodes much faster than it would alone. This is **galvanic** (bimetallic) corrosion. The danger is greatest for a small part made of the weaker metal: a zinc-plated steel screw in stainless steel trunking, for example, can rust away while the trunking still looks new. Use the fixings, washers and earth links the maker supplies for that system, and stainless fixings with stainless trunking.

Galvanising coats steel with zinc. The zinc corrodes slowly in place of the steel. Wherever you cut or drill, bare steel is exposed. Indoors in a dry room the zinc beside the cut gives some protection, but in damp or coastal places treat every cut edge with zinc-rich paint, as the maker says.

sections.title: Planning: survey, route, take-off, cost and safety

ul: Check that you have the **latest revision** of each drawing and the specification.

Find the trunking type, size and finish; the route and the height above **finished floor level (FFL)**; the fill limit and any spare capacity; which systems share the trunking; the fire-rated walls and floors; the earthing method; and the tests and records the client wants.
If two documents disagree, for example the plan and the elevation give different heights, do not guess and do not split the difference. Raise a written query and wait for a written answer.

head: Look for
Why it matters
rows: Wall and ceiling materials: block, concrete, drywall, timber, steel
They decide the fixings and the drilling method.
Obstacles: columns, doors, windows, pipes, ducts, sprinklers
They decide the bends and sets, and may move the route.
Fire-rated walls and floors
Every crossing needs a fire barrier inside and fire stopping outside.
Building expansion joints
The trunking needs a sliding joint there.
Existing cables and pipes hidden in the walls
Scan before drilling; plan isolations.
Heat, sun, damp and salt air
They decide the material and finish.
Access and height
They decide between steps, a podium, a tower or a work platform.
Other trades' progress: floors, ceilings, painting
It decides when you can fix.

ul: Run straight, level or plumb, and parallel to the building's lines.
Keep the **lid removable along the whole run**, so that cables can be added or inspected later. Do not box the trunking in behind pipes, ducts or shelving.
Use as few bends as the job allows, and leave room at each bend for the largest cable's bending radius.
Keep clear of heat and of places where water could drip or collect.
Heights are measured from the finished floor. If the tiles or screed are not laid, add their thickness to the height you mark from the slab.
Surface trunking in a room that is being decorated is normally fixed **after painting**, unless the plan says otherwise, so the paint is not spoiled and the trunking is not painted over.

blocks.p: A **take-off** is the list of every item and quantity, measured from the drawings. Measure each run to scale and check it on site if you can. Count every fitting, coupler, outlet box and end cap, then the fixings. Add a waste allowance for off-cuts (about 10% is common for straight lengths) and **round up** to whole lengths.

blocks.note: **Example.** The runs on the drawing are 9.6 m, 7.2 m and 4.1 m. Total = 20.9 m. With 10% waste: 20.9 × 1.1 = 22.99 m. The trunking comes in 3 m lengths: 22.99 ÷ 3 = 7.66, so order **8 lengths**. Always round up: 7 lengths would leave you short.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Item
Quantity
Unit price
Cost
rows: 50 × 50 mm trunking, 3 m lengths
Angles
Tee
Outlet boxes
End caps
Total for these items

blocks.p: The prices above are made up for the example. To the total you add couplers, earth links, fixings and any other items, then the firm's mark-up as its policy says, and GCT at the current rate. Set the take-off out as a table like this one so that someone else can check it, and check it yourself with a rough estimate: 8 lengths at about J$3,500 is about J$28,000, so J$27,200 is sensible.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Live circuits in existing trunking, or in the wall you will drill
Find out which circuits are there and which boards feed them. Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead before opening the trunking or drilling beside it.
Hidden cables and pipes
Check the drawings and scan with a cable and pipe detector before every hole.
Work at height
For a job of more than a few minutes, use a podium, mobile tower or work platform, not a ladder, chair or crate.
Dust from drilling concrete and block
The fine dust contains silica, which damages the lungs. Use dust extraction on the drill and wear a suitable dust mask.
Noise from hammer drills and saws
Ear protection.
Sharp edges on cut steel
Cut-resistant gloves; file every edge at once.
Long, heavy steel lengths
Two people to carry and lift; plan how lengths reach high-level runs.
People below or beside the work
Barriers and signs; agree work times in occupied buildings.
Sparks from cut-off saws and grinders
Use only if allowed, with the site's hot-work rules; a hacksaw is the normal tool.

flow: Read the drawings and specification; raise queries
Survey the route
Check capacity; prepare the take-off and order
Write the method and risk assessment; brief the team
Isolate where needed; mark out
Fix the trunking; make joints and bends; fit earth links
Test earth continuity (steel)
Hold point: inspect before cables go in
Lay in cables; hold point before lids go on
Final inspection, labels, as-built drawing and handover

blocks.p: Two separate questions decide how many cables a trunking may hold. **Will they fit**, with room to lay them in without damage? And **will they stay cool enough** to carry their current? You answer the first; the designer answers the second, but you must know when to ask.

ul: Inside area of the trunking = inside width × inside depth.
Area of one cable = 3.14 × d × d ÷ 4, where d is the cable's **overall** diameter, including its insulation. Cable data sheets give d.
Total cable area must be no more than the fill limit × the inside area.
Percentage fill = total cable area ÷ inside area × 100.

blocks.p: The fill limit comes from the specification. British practice commonly allows **45%** for trunking. The NEC limits a wireway to **20%** of its cross-section. Never assume: read the specification.

blocks.note: **Example.** A trunking is 100 × 50 mm inside: area = 5,000 mm². At a 45% limit the cables may take up 0.45 × 5,000 = 2,250 mm². Each cable is 5.0 mm across: area = 3.14 × 5 × 5 ÷ 4 = 19.6 mm². Number of cables = 2,250 ÷ 19.6 = 114.8, so **114 cables** (round down). If the specification said 20%, the limit would be 1,000 mm² and only 51 cables.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Makers and installation guides give every cable size a **cable factor** and every trunking size a **trunking factor**. The trunking factor already allows for the fill limit. Add up the cable factors: the total must not be more than the trunking factor.

head: Cable (example figures)
Cable factor
Trunking (example figures)
Trunking factor
rows: 1.5 mm²
2.5 mm²
4 mm²
6 mm²

blocks.p: **Example.** A run must hold 24 cables of 2.5 mm² and 9 cables of 6 mm², and the specification asks for 25% spare capacity. Cable factors: 24 × 12 = 288 and 9 × 22 = 198; total **486**. The 38 × 38 mm trunking (570) would hold them, but 486 ÷ 570 = 85% of its capacity is used, leaving only 15% spare. The 50 × 50 mm trunking (1,037) is 486 ÷ 1,037 = 47% used, leaving more than half spare. Choose **50 × 50 mm**.

blocks.note: The figures in the table are examples for practice only. Real factors depend on the cable's make and insulation: use the table in the specification or the maker's catalogue.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: '25% spare' means that a quarter of the capacity is left free for future cables, so today's cables may use no more than 75% of it. With a trunking factor of 1,037, today's total must not pass 0.75 × 1,037 = 777. Spare space is what makes trunking worth its cost: the client can add circuits for years without new containment.

ul: Every loaded cable makes heat. A cable clipped on its own loses that heat to the air. Cables bunched in trunking warm each other and cannot lose heat as easily.

So the more loaded cables share a trunking, the **less current each may carry**. The designer applies a **grouping factor** from the code's tables, and a second factor where the surroundings are hot, such as a roof space.
This can force a larger cable size than the load alone would need. That in turn takes more space, so capacity is checked again.

Codes differ on when grouping factors begin. Under the NEC, for example, they apply in a wireway only when it holds more than 30 current-carrying conductors and the 20% fill is kept. The designer decides; your job is to give the true number of cables.

**Adding circuits to an existing trunking changes the grouping for every cable already in it.** A run that is under its fill limit may still need the designer's check before more loaded circuits go in.

blocks.p: If the cables will not fit within the limit, the answer is a larger size, a second run, or a different route for some circuits, agreed with the designer and the client. It is never to squeeze the cables in, leave the lid off, or run cables loose on top of the lid: a pinched cable is a fault waiting to happen, and an open trunking protects nothing.

head: Reason
What could go wrong
rows: Safety
A fault in a power cable could put mains voltage onto a data or control cable, and so onto equipment and people who expect only a few volts.
Interference
The magnetic fields round power cables cause electrical noise in data and signal cables: errors, slow networks and false readings.
Keeping life-safety systems working
A fault or fire in the power cables must not knock out the fire alarm or the emergency lighting.
Maintenance
A worker opening a labelled data compartment must not meet a power cable.

head: System
How it is run
rows: 110 V and 220 V power and lighting
May share a compartment, as long as **every cable is insulated for the highest voltage present**. Check the voltage rating printed on the cable.
Data, telephone, CCTV and other signal cables
Their own compartment, with a continuous divider, or a separate trunking at the distance the specification gives. A solid metal divider often lets them run side by side.
Fire alarm
Its own compartment or its own route, in fire-resistant cable, exactly as the alarm design says.
Emergency lighting
Kept apart from other circuits as the design says, in fire-resistant cable where specified.
Generator-backed or UPS circuits
Labelled clearly, because they can stay live when the JPS supply is off.

ul: The divider must **continue through every bend, tee, angle and outlet box**. Use the fittings made for that multi-compartment system: a gap in the divider at a corner defeats the whole run.
Cables do not cross from one compartment to another. Where a route really must cross, use the maker's crossover fitting, which keeps the systems apart.
Outlets for different systems go in separate boxes, or in a box with a divider.
Data cables have their own minimum bending radius, often about four times the cable's diameter. Tight corners damage their performance, so use the large-radius fittings in data compartments.
**Label each compartment at access points** (for example 'POWER', 'DATA', 'FIRE ALARM'), so the next person keeps the systems apart.

blocks.p: A fire-rated wall or floor is built to hold back fire and smoke for a stated time, so that people can escape and the fire stays in one part of the building. A trunking that passes through it makes two openings: the gap **round the outside** of the trunking and the space **inside** it. Both must be sealed.

flow: Find the fire-rated walls and floors on the drawing
Agree the crossing point and the fire-stop product
Fit the fire barrier inside the trunking at the wall
Seal the gap round the trunking with the approved fire stopping
Photograph and record it before ceilings are closed
Make it good again every time cables are added

blocks.note: Fire stopping is a tested system: a named product, used in the way its maker tested it, for that kind of wall and that kind of opening. Ordinary expanding foam, silicone sealant or a handful of mortar is not fire stopping. Use only what the specification approves, and follow the product's instructions exactly.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: When extra cables are laid through a fire barrier, the barrier is disturbed. **Making it good is part of the job**, not an extra: the wall has no fire rating until it is done.
PVC trunking softens and burns away in a fire, leaving a hole. Its crossing of a fire wall needs the method the fire-stop maker gives for plastic services.
On escape routes such as corridors and stairs, the specification may forbid PVC trunking or ask for low-smoke materials, because smoke and fumes are what stop people getting out.

blocks.p: A Level 3 electrician does not measure each piece as it comes. Measure the whole run, draw a cutting plan, and mark every length from it. This lets you place the joints where you want them, use full lengths where you can, and get more than one piece out of each length.

blocks.note: **Example.** Wall A is 7.4 m and wall B is 4.5 m; the trunking comes in 3 m lengths. Cut wall by wall, you use 3 + 3 + 1.4 m, then 3 + 1.5 m: five lengths, with two big off-cuts. Planned together, the third length gives the 1.4 m piece for wall A **and** the 1.5 m piece for wall B (2.9 m in all), so **four lengths** do both walls.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Set a level line from a fixed datum with a laser level, or a spirit level and chalk line. Do not measure up from an uneven floor at each fixing.
Say on the plan whether the line is the top or the bottom edge of the trunking, so the whole team works to the same edge.
Keep joints away from outlet positions and close to a fixing.
Place the **lid joints away from the base joints**, so that each lid bridges a base joint and stiffens it.
Fittings take up part of the run. The maker's instructions say how far short of a corner the trunking must stop: measure to that point.

head: Material
Method
rows: PVC
Fine-tooth hacksaw, with the trunking held in a mitre box for true 90° and 45° cuts
Light, steady strokes; coarse teeth chip thin PVC
Trim off the plastic whiskers with a file or deburring tool
Steel
Hacksaw with a fine blade (about 32 teeth per 25 mm), so that several teeth are on the thin metal at once
Clamp the work and support the off-cut
File off **every burr**, inside and out, straight away
Treat cut edges of galvanised trunking where the conditions need it
Round holes with a hole saw or punch; fit a grommet or bush in every one

blocks.note: A burr left inside steel trunking is a blade pointing at the cables. It may cut through the insulation as the cables are laid in, or months later as they move with heat and vibration. Wear cut-resistant gloves and safety glasses, and check every cut end with a gloved finger before the piece goes up.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Point
Factory fitting
Site-made bend
rows: Good points
Correct radius; dividers continue; neat and identical every time; quick to fit
Any angle; no waiting for a fitting; uses trunking you already have
Weak points
Costs more per piece; must be ordered in time
Needs skill and time; edges, strength and earth continuity depend on the worker
Best for
PVC and dado systems, multi-compartment trunking, data compartments, public areas, and any job with many bends
A single bend in steel trunking, an odd angle, or an urgent job where no fitting can be had

blocks.p: For PVC, use the maker's moulded bends and angles. Where a site joint cannot be avoided, mitre both pieces at half the angle of the turn (45° each for a 90° turn). Do not try to bend PVC trunking with heat: it distorts, the lid no longer fits and the divider is lost.
Every site-made bend follows one idea: **cut away the metal that would overlap, bend the metal that can bend, and back the joint with a plate.** Which part you cut depends on which way the run turns.

head: Bend
What happens to the metal
Method
rows: Flat bend, as the unit calls the usual site-made 90° bend
The metal that would overlap on the inside of the turn is cut away

Mark and cut a V out of the side walls at the bend line, fold the base, and fix a backing plate across the joint with rivets or bolts. If the run must turn in the plane of the wall, the base is mitred instead and joined with a backing plate. Your instructor shows the Centre's method.
Internal angle: the run turns into an inside corner
The base folds, and the two side walls would overlap
Cut matching V notches out of both side walls, with their points at the fold line on the base. Fold the base and back the joint.
External angle: the run turns round an outside corner
The base folds the other way, and the side walls open up
Cut both side walls straight down to the base at the fold line. Fold the base, then rivet filler pieces into the gaps in the side walls.

ul: Mark the cuts with a try square and scriber from measured lines. A V that is off-centre gives a twisted bend.
File every cut edge smooth before and after bending.
The backing plate makes the joint strong and helps the earth path. Bolt or rivet it on clean metal, and still test the joint.
Make the lid for the bend from mitred pieces of lid, or use the factory lid for that bend.
Check that the largest cable can turn through the bend without being forced tighter than its minimum bending radius. If it cannot, the bend needs a sweep or a factory fitting.

blocks.note: Books and makers do not all use the same names for bends. Before you cut, be clear which way the run turns and which part of the trunking must fold. Your instructor will show you the Centre's method.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Fixing, joining, expansion and laying in cables

head: Fixing to
Use
rows: Block wall
Wall plugs with round-head screws and washers. The washer spreads the load so the screw does not pull through or crack the base.
Concrete
Plugs or anchors chosen for the load, set to the maker's depth in a clean hole.
Drywall
Cavity fixings, or screws into the studs. Plain plugs pull out.
Structural steel
Beam clamps or the fixing the specification gives. Do not drill structural steel without the engineer's approval.
Below a roof or slab
Drop rods (threaded rod) anchored to the structure, with brackets under the trunking. Never hang trunking from ceiling grids, pipes, sprinkler lines or ducts.

ul: **Support spacing comes from the maker's data for that size and load**, not from habit. As a rough guide only, small PVC trunking is fixed about every half metre, and steel trunking from under a metre for small sizes to about three metres for large ones.
Put a fixing close to each joint, bend and tee, and near each end.
On an uneven wall, **pack behind the base** so that it sits straight. A base pulled into a hollow twists, and the lid springs off.
On vertical runs, fit pin racks or retainers at intervals so that the cables' weight is carried by the trunking, not by their terminations.
Check each length with a level as it is fixed. An error in the first length is copied by every length after it.
Butt the lengths together in line and fit the coupler or joint cover the maker supplies.
On steel, fix the coupler with all its screws and fit the earth link (see the next section).
Fit factory tees and angles with their own couplers. A tee has three joints: each one is joined and linked.
Enter a distribution board with a **flanged adaptor** bolted to both the board and the trunking. It covers the cut edges, keeps dust and vermin out and bonds the trunking to the board.
Never pass cables through a rough hole or a ragged slot, and never leave a gap between the trunking and the board.
Where conduit leaves the trunking, use a proper connector and bush. Where a cable leaves through a hole, fit a grommet or bush.
Close unused holes so the enclosure keeps its protection.

blocks.p: Everything grows when it heats. PVC grows about five or six times as much as steel. Typical figures are about **0.07 mm per metre for each 1 °C** for PVC and about **0.012 mm** for steel; the maker gives the real figure.

blocks.note: **Example.** A 20 m PVC run warms by 30 °C between a cool night and a hot afternoon. Change in length = 20 × 30 × 0.07 = **42 mm**. A steel run in the same place changes by 20 × 30 × 0.012 = about 7 mm. If the PVC cannot move, it bows off the wall or pulls out its fixings.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: On long PVC runs in hot places, use **expansion couplers** or leave the gap at each joint that the maker's chart gives for the temperature on the day.
Fix so that the lengths can slide: do not screw both ends of every length down hard where the maker gives slotted fixing holes.

Where a run crosses a **building expansion joint**, fit a sliding joint, and on steel trunking a **flexible earth link** across it, so the two parts of the building can move without tearing the run or breaking the earth path.
Leave a little slack in the cables at each expansion joint.

flow: Hold point: inside clean, no burrs or swarf, joints and links complete, continuity tested
Fit retainers on vertical runs and where the lid faces down
Lay cables in straight, system by system, without twists or crossings
Keep each cable's bending radius at bends and exits
Label the cables and check the fill
Hold point: no cable pinched, dividers in place, labels on
Fit and fix the lids along the whole run

blocks.p: Cables in a ceiling run with the lid facing down will fall out as fast as you lay them unless retainers go in first. Tape is not a retainer: it dries out and lets go. Before any lid goes on, run a hand along the edge of the base to make sure no cable is sitting on it, because a lid forced over a cable cuts into it.

sections.title: Earth continuity and testing of steel trunking

flow: A cable's insulation is damaged and the line conductor touches the trunking
Fault current flows along the trunking and the earth conductor back to the board
The path has a very low resistance, so the current is large
The breaker or fuse opens quickly
The trunking is no longer live

blocks.p: Now suppose one joint is loose, painted or rusty. The fault current is held back by that joint's resistance. It may be too small to open the breaker quickly, or at all. Every length beyond the bad joint then sits at a dangerous voltage, and the first person to touch it and something earthed completes the circuit.

ul: Some designs use the steel trunking itself as the protective (earth) conductor for the circuits inside. This is allowed only where the code and the specification permit it, every joint is made reliably continuous, and the result is tested.

Many specifications ask for a **separate protective conductor in each circuit as well**. The trunking must still be earthed and its joints linked, because a damaged cable can touch the trunking whether or not it has its own earth.
PVC trunking does not conduct, so it needs no earthing; every circuit in it carries its own protective conductor.
Fit an **earth link** (a copper strap, usually tinned) across **every joint**: each coupler, each joint of a tee or cross, each bend, and the flange at the board.
Bolt the link to **clean, bare metal** on both sides, with the serrated washers supplied. Paint, dirt and loose bolts are the usual causes of a bad joint.
Do not rely on the coupler screws alone unless the maker states that the coupler gives earth continuity.
Use a flexible link at expansion joints.
Connect the run to the **earth bar of the distribution board** with a conductor of the size the specification gives. A nearby water pipe, or contact with the wall, is not an earth connection.

blocks.p: Use a **low-resistance ohmmeter**, which may be one function of a multifunction installation tester. Do the test after the run is complete and **before the cables go in**, when a bad joint is still easy to reach.

flow: Confirm the run is dead and no circuit is connected
Check the instrument and its calibration date
Null (zero) the test leads, so their own resistance is not counted
Measure from the board's earth bar to the far end of the run, and to the end of each branch
If a reading is high, measure across each joint to find the bad one
Clean, refit the link, tighten and retest
Record the readings

head: Measured across (example readings)
Reading
What it tells you
rows: Joint 1
Good
Joint 2
Good
Joint 3
Far higher than the others: link missing, loose or on paint
Joint 4
Good
Earth bar to far end
High, because of joint 3

ul: A sound run reads a small fraction of an ohm, and every joint reads about the same. The test sheet or specification gives the limit to work to.
**One reading that stands out from the rest marks the fault**, even if the total looks small.
Looking at a joint, or pulling on it, proves nothing. Only the instrument proves continuity.
Near the sea, joints corrode with time. Continuity is tested again during maintenance.

blocks.p: Write the results on the test record, not on a scrap of paper or inside the lid. The record shows the run tested, the readings end to end and at any joint that was reworked, the instrument's make and serial number and its calibration date, the tester's name, the date and a signature. A record lets the inspector accept the work, and lets a later electrician see whether a joint has got worse.

sections.title: Inspection, handover and leading the team

head: Area
Check
rows: Route and position
Right route and height against the drawing; level and plumb; lid removable along the whole run.
Fixings
Right type for the wall; maker's spacing; fixings near joints, bends and ends; nothing loose.
Cuts and joints
Cut edges smooth, no burrs; joints tight with no gaps; cut edges treated where needed.
Fittings
Bends, tees and end caps fitted; site-made bends strong and smooth; room for the cables' bending radius.
Cables
Not over the fill limit; none pinched, cut or strained; retainers on vertical and lid-down runs.
Segregation
Dividers continuous through every fitting; each system in its own compartment; compartments labelled.
Exits and entries
Grommets or bushes at every hole; flanged adaptor at the board; unused holes closed.
Fire safety
Fire barriers inside and fire stopping outside at every fire-rated wall and floor; photographs taken.
Earthing (steel)
Earth link at every joint; connection to the earth bar; continuity tested and recorded.
Finish
Lids fitted and fixed along the whole length; area clean; off-cuts removed.

head: Kind of defect
Examples
Action
rows: Safety defect
Cable insulation cut or pinched
A sharp edge or missing grommet where a cable passes
Missing earth link or high continuity reading
Missing fire stopping
Power and data mixed in one compartment
Must be put right and rechecked **before any circuit is energised**.
Workmanship defect
A small gap at a lid joint
A run slightly out of level
A missing label
Put right before handover. It does not stop testing, but it is not left for the client to find.

blocks.p: A damaged cable is replaced, not taped: tape does not restore the insulation, and the cause of the damage, such as a burr, must be removed as well. Write every defect on a **snag list** with its location, the action needed, who will do it, the date it was done and who rechecked it.

ul: The **as-built drawing**, marked with the true routes and sizes, the compartments, the fire-stop positions and every change from the design. Later workers rely on it to find cables without guessing, and to avoid drilling into them.
The earth continuity test record and the inspection checklist, signed.
Photographs of work that will be hidden, such as fire stopping above a ceiling.
The maker's data for the trunking system, including its capacity, so the client knows how much spare space remains.
Vacuum swarf and filings out of the trunking and off the floor. Steel filings left in trunking can work into cable insulation.
Sort the off-cuts: steel goes for scrap, PVC into the waste the site provides.
**Never burn PVC off-cuts.** Burning PVC gives off hydrogen chloride and other toxic fumes.
Return tools and test instruments, and report anything damaged.

flow: Brief: drawing, route, heights, fittings and the standard expected
Safety briefing: isolation, scanning, access, dust, PPE
Show a good joint and a good cut
Share the work so each person learns; pair the least experienced with you
Check each person's first piece before they carry on
Hold points before cables go in and before lids go on
Give clear feedback; have defects corrected; record the checks

ul: A **first-piece check** matters because a fault you catch on the first length is corrected once. A fault you find at the end has been repeated along the whole run.

When a trainee gets something wrong, such as leaving out earth links, have the work corrected and then tested. Explain why it matters, and check that the trainee can now do it. Tearing the whole run down, or quietly doing it yourself, teaches nothing.
Never sign a checklist or test record for work you have not checked yourself.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the main types of trunking and say where each is the best choice.
I can name the common fittings and say what each one does.
I can choose a material for a kitchen, a sea-front wall, a sunny outdoor wall and an air-conditioned office, and explain my choice.
I can explain galvanic corrosion and why matching fixings are used.
I can find what I need in a drawing and specification, and raise a query when documents disagree.
I can survey a route and list what must be found out before work starts.
I can prepare a take-off with a waste allowance, round up to whole lengths and cost it.
I can work out the inside area of a trunking, the most cable area it may hold and its percentage fill.
I can use cable factors and a trunking factor to choose a size with spare capacity.
I can explain why grouped cables carry less current, and why the designer must be asked before circuits are added to an existing run.
I can explain why systems are segregated, and how dividers, outlet boxes and labels keep them apart.
I can describe how trunking is sealed inside and outside at a fire-rated wall, and why it must be made good after changes.
I can plan cuts from one measured plan to reduce waste.
I can cut PVC and steel trunking square and leave no burrs.
I can decide between a factory fitting and a site-made bend, and describe how a site-made bend is cut, bent and backed.
I can choose fixings for different walls and say where the support spacing comes from.
I can work out how much a long run will expand and say how to allow for it.
I can explain why steel trunking is earthed, fit earth links correctly and connect the run to the earth bar.
I can test earth continuity with a low-resistance ohmmeter, find a bad joint and record the results.
I can inspect a finished job, sort safety defects from workmanship defects and keep a snag list.
I can put together a handover pack with an as-built drawing.
I can brief, supervise and check a team, using first-piece checks and hold points.

head: What
How
rows: Inside area of trunking
Inside width × inside depth (mm²)
Area of one cable
3.14 × d × d ÷ 4, with d the overall diameter
Most cable area allowed
Fill limit × inside area
Percentage fill
Total cable area ÷ inside area × 100
Cable factor method
Total of the cable factors must not be more than the trunking factor
Lengths to order
Total run × (1 + waste allowance) ÷ length of one piece, rounded up
Expansion
Length (m) × temperature change (°C) × the maker's figure (mm per m per °C)
Common fill limits
45% in British practice for trunking; 20% for an NEC wireway; the specification decides
Typical expansion
PVC about 0.07 mm per m per °C; steel about 0.012 mm per m per °C

terms: As-built drawing
The drawing marked up to show how the work was actually installed, including every change.
Backing plate
A plate riveted or bolted across the joint of a site-made bend to make it strong.
Burr
The sharp, rough edge left on metal after cutting or drilling.
Cable factor
A number from a maker's or guide's table, given to each cable size, used to work out how many cables fit.
Cable retainer
A strap or bridge that holds cables in the trunking when the lid is off, faces down or the run is vertical.
Dado trunking
Trunking fitted along a wall at about desk height, often with separate compartments for power and data.
Divider
The part inside multi-compartment trunking that keeps the compartments apart.
Drop rod
A threaded steel rod fixed to the structure, used to hang trunking below a ceiling or roof.
Earth link
A copper strap bolted across a joint in steel trunking to keep the earth path continuous.
Fill limit (space factor)
The largest share of the trunking's inside area that the cables may take up.
Fire barrier
A seal fitted inside trunking where it passes through a fire-rated wall or floor.
Fire stopping
A tested, approved seal round services where they pass through a fire-rated wall or floor.
Finished floor level (FFL)
The level of the floor surface when the building is complete; heights on drawings are measured from it.
Flanged adaptor
The fitting that joins trunking to a distribution board or box.
Galvanic corrosion
Fast corrosion of one metal where two different metals touch in damp or salty air.
Galvanising
Coating steel with zinc to protect it from rust.
Grouping factor
A factor that lowers a cable's current rating when it runs with other loaded cables.
Hold point
A stage where work stops until it has been checked and accepted.
Low-resistance ohmmeter
The instrument used to test earth continuity.
Segregation
Keeping different systems, such as power, data and fire alarm, apart.
Snag list
A list of defects with their locations, the action needed and who rechecked them.
Take-off
The list of all the materials for a job, with quantities, prepared from the drawings.
Trunking factor
A number from a maker's or guide's table for each trunking size; the total of the cable factors must not exceed it.
UV (ultraviolet)
The part of sunlight that makes ordinary plastics brittle.

c1.title: A computer lab at a college in Mona
c1.text: Kadeem Brown, a Level 3 trainee, leads three Level 2 trainees fitting two-compartment PVC dado trunking round a new 32-seat computer lab at a college in Mona, St Andrew. The drawing puts the bottom edge of the trunking 900 mm above finished floor level. The floor tiles are not laid yet: they and their bedding will raise the floor 25 mm above the level slab. The specification asks for 25% spare capacity in each compartment. The maker's table gives a trunking factor of 860 for the power compartment and a cable factor of 12 for each 2.5 mm² cable. The college's alarm contractor also wants a route along the same walls for a fire alarm sounder cable.

c2.title: Steel trunking above a filling line in Bog Walk
c2.text: Shereece Gordon, a Level 3 electrician, leads a team installing 100 × 100 mm galvanised steel trunking along a block wall, 3.2 m above the filling line of a juice factory in Bog Walk, St Catherine. The run has a site-made bend, a factory tee and a flanged entry into the top of a distribution board. The specification says every circuit has its own protective (earth) conductor, and the trunking must also be earthed and tested. One cable in the run is a 32 mm armoured sub-main whose data sheet gives a minimum bending radius of 6 times its diameter. Open bottles pass along the line below during both shifts.

c3.title: A seafood restaurant at Treasure Beach
c3.text: Mr Leon Walters, a Level 3 electrician, is planning the trunking for a seafood restaurant at Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth, about 40 m from the sea. The kitchen has a gas range under an extract canopy, and the specification calls for stainless steel trunking there. The bar is open-sided, and an 18 m run must go along its back wall, which faces west into the afternoon sun. The owner has bought white indoor PVC mini-trunking and zinc-plated steel screws at a hardware sale and wants them used everywhere to save money.

c4.title: New circuits in a bank branch in St Ann's Bay
c4.text: Ms Tamara Reid, a Level 3 electrician, must add six 110 V circuits for new teller counters at a bank branch in St Ann's Bay, St Ann. They will run in an existing three-compartment steel trunking: power circuits from two distribution boards share one compartment, data has the second and the fire alarm the third. The trunking passes through a fire-rated wall into the strongroom corridor. The power compartment is 38% full and the specification allows 45%. The bank stays open on weekdays, so the work is planned for a Saturday afternoon.

c5.title: Final inspection at a health clinic in Lucea
c5.text: Mr Andre Thompson, a Level 3 electrician, is making the final inspection of a new trunking system at a health clinic in Lucea, Hanover. His snag list so far has four items: a 2 mm gap at a lid joint in the waiting room; a cable whose insulation is nicked where it lies across a burr on a steel coupler; a cable that leaves the trunking through a rough drilled hole into a switch drop; and a 3 m section that was dropped 400 mm lower than the drawing shows, to pass under a new air-conditioning duct.

questions.q: The power compartment must hold 21 circuits, each with three 2.5 mm² cables. Does this meet the specification?
o: Yes: the total of 756 is under the trunking factor of 860
No: the total of 756 is over the 645 allowed with 25% spare
Yes: the total of 252 is far below the trunking factor of 860
No: the total of 756 is over a quarter of 860, which is 215
questions.why: There are 21 × 3 = 63 cables, and 63 × 12 = 756. With 25% kept spare, today's cables may use only 75% of 860, which is 645. The cables would physically fit, but the spare capacity the client is paying for would be gone, so a larger size or a second run is needed.

questions.q: At what height above the bare slab should the team mark the bottom edge of the trunking?
o: 875 mm
900 mm
950 mm
925 mm
questions.why: Drawing heights are measured from finished floor level. The tiles and bedding will raise the floor by 25 mm, so the mark goes 900 + 25 = 925 mm above the slab. Marked at 900 mm, every outlet in the lab would end up 25 mm too low.

questions.q: The alarm contractor asks to lay the sounder cable in the data compartment, which has plenty of room. What should Kadeem tell him?
o: It needs its own segregated route, as the alarm design says
It may go there, as both systems carry extra-low voltage
It may go there if it is tied along one side of the compartment
It should go in the power compartment, beside the divider
questions.why: A fire alarm must keep working when other systems fail or burn, so its cables are kept apart from all others, in the cable type and on the route its design gives. Spare room in another compartment does not change that. Kadeem should refer the request to the designer.

questions.q: Kadeem inspects each trainee's first fixed length before letting that trainee carry on. Why is this the best moment for the check?
o: The college must sign for every length as soon as it is fixed
A length cannot be taken down once the next one is joined
A fault is put right before it is repeated along the wall
It means the finished run will not need a final inspection
questions.why: An error in height, level, fixings or cutting is copied by every length that follows. Caught on the first piece, it is corrected once and the trainee learns the standard. A first-piece check never replaces the hold points or the final inspection.

questions.q: Each circuit has its own earth conductor. Why must the steel trunking still have an earth link across every joint?
o: The links carry part of the neutral current back to the board
The links hold the joints tight so the lids fit along the run
The links stop the galvanised joints rusting in damp air
A cable fault to the trunking must still trip the breaker
questions.why: A damaged cable can touch the steel whether or not its circuit has its own earth. The fault current needs an unbroken, low-resistance path along the trunking so that the breaker opens quickly. A bad joint could leave every length beyond it live.

questions.q: With no circuits connected, the team measures 0.04 Ω from the earth bar to the tee, but 0.90 Ω from the earth bar to the far end. Every joint reads about 0.01 Ω except the one just past the tee, at 0.86 Ω. What should be done?
o: Clean that joint to bare metal, refit its link and retest
Record 0.90 Ω as a pass, since it is still well below one ohm
Fit a second link at the board end to lower the total
Coat that joint with zinc-rich paint and test it again
questions.why: One joint that reads far higher than the rest is the fault: its link is missing, loose or sitting on paint or dirt. Clean it, refit and tighten the link, then retest and record. Adding links elsewhere, or more paint, leaves the bad joint in the fault path.

questions.q: What is the smallest bending radius the bend in the run must allow for the armoured sub-main?
o: 32 mm
192 mm
38 mm
384 mm
questions.why: Minimum radius = 6 × the overall diameter = 6 × 32 = 192 mm. A sharp square corner would force the cable tighter than this and damage it, so the bend needs a sweep or a fitting with enough room.

questions.q: Cutting and drilling will be needed directly above the open bottles on the line. Which control is best?
o: Give the team dust masks, so that the dust can do no harm
Drill at full speed, so that each hole makes less dust
Blow the swarf off the trunking with compressed air
Cut away from the line, and sheet off below the drilling
questions.why: The best control removes the hazard: do the cutting and filing somewhere else, agree times with the factory, and catch drilling dust with extraction and sheeting. Masks protect only the wearer, and steel filings or dust in an open bottle are a danger to the public.

questions.q: Which trunking is the best choice for the 18 m run on the bar's west-facing wall?
o: The owner's indoor PVC, with tape over each lid joint
Plain mild steel trunking, given a coat of house paint
Outdoor-grade UV-resistant PVC, with stainless fixings
The owner's indoor PVC, fixed with zinc-plated screws
questions.why: The wall gets strong sun and salt air. UV makes indoor PVC brittle, and plain steel and zinc-plated screws rust quickly near the sea. A PVC made and marked for outdoor use, or stainless steel, with stainless fixings, will last.

questions.q: The 18 m PVC run will be much hotter in the afternoon than at night. How should its joints be made?
o: Glued solid, so that the run moves as one piece
With expansion couplers or gaps, as the maker's chart says
Butted hard together, and screwed down firmly at both ends
Left open by 50 mm, with the cables bridging each gap
questions.why: At about 0.07 mm per metre per °C, an 18 m PVC run changes by tens of millimetres between night and a hot afternoon. If it cannot move, it bows or pulls its fixings out. Expansion couplers, or the gap the maker gives, let each length slide while the cables stay enclosed.

questions.q: The kitchen trunking must get past the gas range to reach the extract fan's isolator. Which plan is best?
o: Stainless trunking routed clear of the range's hot zone
The owner's PVC mini-trunking, fixed just above the range
PVC mini-trunking with its lid glued to keep the grease out
Any trunking, because the canopy removes all of the heat
questions.why: PVC softens and warps with heat, and a canopy does not keep the wall behind a range cool. Steel or stainless steel stands the conditions, but even metal trunking is routed away from the hottest zone, because heat also lowers the current the cables can carry.

questions.q: Why should the owner's zinc-plated screws not be used to fix the stainless steel trunking?
o: Zinc-plated screws are too soft to grip in a block wall
Stainless trunking cannot be earthed through steel screws
The screws would make the trunking's lid hard to remove
The screws would corrode quickly against the stainless
questions.why: Two different metals touching in salty, damp air cause galvanic corrosion, and the small part of the weaker metal suffers most. The screws could rust through while the trunking still looks new, and the run would come off the wall. Use stainless fixings with stainless trunking.

questions.q: Before the lid of the power compartment comes off, which circuits must be isolated and proved dead?
o: Only the circuits from the board that will feed the counters
Every circuit in that compartment, from both boards
Only the circuits that run past the new teller counters
None, if the team wear gloves and take care with the lid
questions.why: Working among cables means handling all of them, and any one could be damaged or already faulty. Find out from the drawings and on site which circuits are in the compartment, then isolate, lock off and tag each one at its own board, and prove dead with a tester checked before and after.

questions.q: The six new circuits would bring the power compartment to 44%, still under the limit. Why should Tamara ask the designer before adding them?
o: A compartment at 44% is too full for its lid to be refitted
Data cables must stay 1% clear of the fill limit for power cables
More loaded cables in the group can lower every cable's rating
The designer has to approve the colour of every new cable
questions.why: The fill limit only answers 'will they fit?'. Extra loaded circuits also add heat, so the grouping factor for every cable in the compartment may change, including the ones already there. Only the designer can confirm that the existing and new cable sizes are still adequate.

questions.q: The fire barrier inside the trunking at the strongroom wall had to be taken out to lay in the new cables. How must it be made good?
o: With the approved fire-stop product, used as its maker tested it
With expanding foam from the hardware store, trimmed off flush after
With nothing more, because the steel lid closes the trunking
With sand and cement mortar packed in round the new cables
questions.why: Fire stopping is a tested system: a named product used in the tested way for that wall and opening. Ordinary foam or hand-packed mortar is not, and a steel lid does not stop fire and smoke travelling inside the trunking. Until the barrier is reinstated and recorded, the wall has lost its rating.

questions.q: What is the right way to deal with the cable that is nicked at the coupler?
o: Wrap the nick with insulating tape and note it on the list
Leave it for the insulation test to show whether it matters
Turn the cable over so the nick faces away from the coupler
File off the burr on the coupler and replace the cable
questions.why: Tape does not restore the cable's insulation, and a nick that passes a test today can fail later. The damaged cable is replaced, and the cause, the burr, is removed so the new cable is not cut as well. Then the item is rechecked and signed off on the snag list.

questions.q: Which repair is right for the rough hole where the cable leaves the trunking into the switch drop?
o: Wrap tape round the cable where it passes through the hole
Smooth the edge of the hole and fit a grommet or bush
Fill the hole round the cable with silicone sealant
Open the hole out until the cable no longer touches it
questions.why: A raw metal edge wears through insulation as the cable moves with heat and vibration. The edge is deburred and a grommet or bush is fitted, so the cable bears on a smooth, insulating surface. A bigger hole still has a sharp edge, and it opens the enclosure.

questions.q: Why does it matter that the as-built drawing shows the section that was dropped 400 mm?
o: The client pays a different rate for trunking fixed lower than drawn
The inspector passes only work that matches the first drawing
Later workers can find the cables, and avoid drilling into them
The maker's guarantee covers only runs shown on a drawing
questions.why: People who extend, maintain or drill near the installation years later rely on the as-built drawing. If it still shows the design route, they will look for the trunking, and assume the wall is clear, in the wrong place. Every change from the design is marked.

questions.q: A specification limits trunking fill to 45%. A trunking measuring 100 × 75 mm inside holds cables with a total area of 3,600 mm². What is the fill?
o: 48%, which is over the limit
36%, which is under the limit
45%, which is just on the limit
4.8%, which is far below the limit
questions.why: Inside area = 100 × 75 = 7,500 mm². Fill = 3,600 ÷ 7,500 × 100 = 48%. That is more than 45%, so a larger trunking or a second run is needed; the cables must not be forced in.

questions.q: A take-off lists 16 lengths of steel trunking at J$3,150 each and 6 angles at J$720 each. What do these items cost before GCT?
questions.why: Trunking: 16 × J$3,150 = J$50,400. Angles: 6 × J$720 = J$4,320. Total = J$54,720. Work out each line separately, then add, and check with a rough estimate: 16 × about J$3,000 is J$48,000, plus about J$4,000.
